screens.title: Card taps
screens.text: A university system looks up a student number every time a student taps their card at a venue. New student numbers are issued in increasing order. Which structure would you choose?
screens.reveal: An unsorted list makes every lookup O(n). A plain BST would grow into a chain because the numbers arrive in increasing order. An AVL tree rebalances after each insertion, so every lookup stays O(log n).

screens.title: Goal
screens.text: Identify practical applications of AVL trees and justify the choice from their properties (LO6).

task.stem: What is the worst-case search cost in a plain BST with n keys?
task.hint: This checks that you can justify the choice from the AVL tree’s properties: guaranteed O(log n) search, at the cost of extra work on updates.

options.explanation: Right. A plain BST can become a chain.
O(log n) is the cost in a balanced tree. A plain BST has no balance guarantee.

screens.title: When an AVL tree is a good fit
points: The data must stay in sorted order: an in-order traversal lists it sorted at any time.
The data is searched often, and a guaranteed O(log n) search matters more than the extra work on updates.
Keys may arrive in sorted or nearly sorted order, which would turn a plain BST into a chain.
Examples: a word list for a spell checker, an index of student numbers, a contacts list kept in alphabetical order.

screens.title: What it costs
points: Space: every node stores its height (or balance factor).
Time: insertion and deletion do extra work to update balance factors and rotate.
This is a time and space trade-off: balanced trees take longer on updates but protect against the worst case.
Red-Black trees are another balanced tree with a looser balance rule; you may meet them later.

screens.title: Worked example: a contacts list
steps: Is the data searched often? Yes: names are looked up all day.
Must it stay in order? Yes: the list is shown alphabetically, and an in-order traversal gives that.
Can keys arrive sorted? Yes: contacts are often imported from an alphabetical file, which would make a plain BST a chain.
How often is it updated? A few contacts a day, so the extra rotation work is small.
Conclusion: an AVL tree fits. It keeps names sorted and guarantees O(log n) lookups, at a small cost on updates.

task.stem: A spell checker loads 200,000 words once from a dictionary file sorted A to Z, then looks up every word you type. Is an AVL tree a good choice?
task.hint: This checks that you can recognise a good fit for an AVL tree: data searched often that must stay in sorted order.

options.text: No: a plain BST is just as fast here, because the words are already sorted
options.explanation: Sorted input is the worst case for a plain BST: every word goes right, giving a chain of 200,000 levels.

options.text: Yes: lookups are frequent, and the sorted file would turn a plain BST into a chain, while an AVL tree keeps lookups O(log n)
options.explanation: Right. The sorted input is exactly the case the AVL rule protects against.

options.text: Yes, because AVL search uses the balance factors to find words faster
options.explanation: The choice is right, but the reason is not: search ignores balance factors. Balance keeps the tree short.

task.stem: A system appends a record to a log every second, and the whole log is read from start to end once a day. Is an AVL tree a good choice?
task.hint: This checks that you can recognise a good fit for an AVL tree: data searched often that must stay in sorted order.

options.text: Yes: an AVL tree is always the best structure for storing data
options.explanation: No structure is best for everything. Here the balancing work buys nothing, because nobody searches by key.

options.text: Yes: an AVL tree costs nothing extra compared with a list
options.explanation: Every insertion updates balance factors and may rotate, and every node stores a height.

options.text: No: nothing is searched by key, so a simple list that appends at the end does the job without the balancing work
options.explanation: Right. An AVL tree pays off only when searches by key are frequent.

screens.title: Lesson check
screens.text: One question for each assessment criterion of this lesson’s objective. Each question allows one re-attempt, and the hint is always available.

screens.title: Summary
points: Choose an AVL tree for sorted data that is searched often, especially if keys can arrive in order.
The price: a height in every node and extra work on every update.
If data is rarely searched by key, a simpler structure is better.
